note.explanation: Some reactions proceed only forwards, while others can proceed both forwards and backwards under the same conditions. In a reversible reaction, products can react to form the original reactants.
examples: NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) is an irreversible reaction that goes to completion.
CuSO₄ · 5 H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(g) shows the reversible change between hydrated and anhydrous copper sulphate.
note.checkAnswer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both directions under the same conditions; an irreversible reaction proceeds only in the forward direction.
note.simple: Some changes can go both ways. Other changes go only forwards.
note.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes
steps: Identify whether the reaction can proceed in both directions under the same conditions.
If it proceeds only forwards, call it irreversible and use →.
If products can form reactants again, call it reversible and use ⇌.
Check whether a product escapes or is removed, because this can make a reversible reaction go to completion.
note.answer: It shows that the reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.

options: Reactants form products, and products can form reactants under the same conditions.
All reactants are completely changed into products.
The reaction proceeds only when a product is removed.
The reaction can occur only in an open container.
mcqs.stem: Which description best identifies a reversible reaction?
rationales: This is correct because a reversible reaction can proceed forwards and backwards under the same conditions.
This describes a reaction going to completion, not the usual behaviour of a reversible reaction.
Removing a product can drive a reversible reaction to completion, but it does not define a reversible reaction.
A reversible reaction can occur in a closed container; it does not require an open container.

mcqs.stem: Which symbol does your textbook use to show a reversible reaction?
rationales: This arrow shows a reaction proceeding in one direction, not the reversible symbol.
This is correct because its two half arrowheads point in opposite directions.
This symbol can indicate a gas being produced, but it does not show a reversible reaction.
This symbol can indicate a decrease, but it does not show a reversible reaction.

options: The products react to form the reactants under the same conditions.
The reaction always takes place in an open container.

rationales: This is correct because the products can react among themselves to give back the reactants under the same conditions.
An open container is not what makes a reaction reversible; a gas escaping may instead drive it to completion.
A reversible reaction does form products, which can then form reactants again.
The physical state of the products does not define whether a reaction is reversible.

Calcium oxide changes into a liquid.

mcqs.stem: Why can heating calcium carbonate in an open container force the reaction to go to completion?
rationales: This is correct because carbon dioxide escapes as it forms, preventing the reverse reaction described in the textbook.
The section does not say that calcium oxide melts during this process.
The reaction can still be heated in an open container; the escaping gas is the important change.
Carbon dioxide can react with calcium oxide in a closed container, where it is retained.

The blue hydrated salt changes into a green gas.
The white anhydrous salt loses all its colour permanently.
The salt changes into calcium carbonate.
mcqs.stem: What happens when white anhydrous copper sulphate absorbs moisture from the atmosphere?
rationales: This is correct because it becomes hydrated copper sulphate, which is blue.
The textbook describes a blue solid forming, not a green gas.
The change is reversible: absorbing moisture makes the salt blue again.
Calcium carbonate is a different compound and is not the product of this change.

rationales: Blue is the colour of anhydrous cobalt chloride in the section.
This is correct because hydrated cobalt chloride hexahydrate is pink.
Purple is the colour of cobalt chloride dihydrate, not the hexahydrate.
White is the colour change described for heated copper sulphate, not hydrated cobalt chloride.

options: The dihydrate is purple and the hexahydrate is pink.
The dihydrate is pink and the hexahydrate is purple.

rationales: This is correct: limited moisture forms the purple dihydrate, and further moisture forms the pink hexahydrate.
This reverses the colours given for the two hydrated forms in the textbook.
Blue is the colour of anhydrous cobalt chloride, not both hydrated forms.
The textbook gives purple and pink for these hydrated forms, not white.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
written.finalAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, forward and backward changes continue at equal rates; in static equilibrium, there is no change or movement.

rubric.why: The key feature of dynamic equilibrium is that opposing changes continue at equal rates.
rubric.description: States that forward and backward changes continue at equal rates in dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.how: Mention both directions and that their rates are equal.

rubric.why: This distinguishes static equilibrium from continuing dynamic changes.
rubric.description: Contrasts this with no change or movement in static equilibrium.
rubric.how: State that static equilibrium has no continuing change or movement.

modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, forward and backward changes continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, there is no change or movement.

written.text: Why are some reactions irreversible while others are reversible?
written.finalAnswer: Irreversible reactions proceed only forwards, usually going to completion. Reversible reactions proceed forwards and backwards under the same conditions because their products can react to form the reactants again.

rubric.why: This gives the defining direction of an irreversible reaction.
rubric.description: Explains that an irreversible reaction proceeds only forwards.
rubric.how: State that it moves in the forward direction only.

rubric.why: Going to completion explains the usual outcome of an irreversible reaction.
rubric.description: Notes that an irreversible reaction can go to completion.
rubric.how: Explain that the reactants are converted into products.

rubric.why: A reversible reaction is characterised by reaction in both directions.
rubric.description: Explains that reversible reactions proceed forwards and backwards.
rubric.how: Name both directions.

rubric.why: The ability of products to reform reactants under the same conditions explains reversibility.
rubric.description: Explains that products can react to give the reactants again under the same conditions.
rubric.how: Connect the backward reaction with products forming reactants.

modelAnswer: An irreversible reaction moves in the forward direction only and may go to completion.
In a reversible reaction, the products react among themselves to give back the reactants under the same conditions.
Therefore, a reversible reaction proceeds in both forward and backward directions.

written.text: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?
written.finalAnswer: Combustion reactions generally release a large amount of heat and form products that do not readily react to give back the original reactants under the same conditions, so they proceed effectively in the forward direction.

rubric.why: Combustion releases heat, which helps explain why the reverse change is not readily achieved under the same conditions.
rubric.description: Mentions that combustion releases a large amount of heat.
rubric.how: State that combustion is strongly heat-releasing.

rubric.why: The products do not readily reform the original reactants under ordinary reaction conditions.
rubric.description: Explains that the products do not readily react back to form the reactants.
rubric.how: Describe the reverse reaction as not readily occurring.

rubric.why: Reversibility is judged by whether the backward reaction occurs under the same conditions.
rubric.description: Relates the explanation to the same reaction conditions.
rubric.how: Make clear that the reverse reaction does not readily occur under the conditions of combustion.

rubric.why: The conclusion identifies the reaction as effectively irreversible.
rubric.description: Concludes that combustion proceeds effectively forwards.
rubric.how: State that it is generally irreversible.

modelAnswer: Combustion releases a large amount of heat.
Its products do not readily react to give back the original reactants under the same conditions.
Therefore, combustion reactions generally proceed in the forward direction and are irreversible.

written.text: Can you make an irreversible reaction reversible and vice versa?
written.finalAnswer: A reaction that is irreversible under one set of conditions may become reversible if the conditions are changed so that the products can react to form the reactants. A reversible reaction can be forced to go to completion by removing a product or allowing a gaseous product to escape.

rubric.why: The behaviour of a reaction can depend on its conditions.
rubric.description: States that changing conditions may change the reaction's behaviour.
rubric.how: Refer to a change in reaction conditions.

rubric.why: A backward reaction requires products to form reactants.
rubric.description: Explains how a reaction may become reversible.
rubric.how: Say that products must be able to react to form reactants.

rubric.why: Removing a product can drive a reversible reaction to completion.
rubric.description: Names removal of a product as one way to force completion.
rubric.how: State that a product can be withdrawn from the mixture.

rubric.why: An escaping gaseous product is the other method described in the section.
rubric.description: Names escape of a gaseous product as a way to force completion.
rubric.how: Explain that gas escaping prevents it from reacting back.

modelAnswer: An irreversible reaction may become reversible if the conditions allow its products to react and form the reactants.
A reversible reaction can be forced to go to completion by removing a product from the reaction mixture.
If a product is a gas, it can escape into the atmosphere and the reaction is forced to go to completion.

written.text: How do you know if a reaction is reversible or irreversible?
written.finalAnswer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both forward and backward directions under the same conditions and is shown by ⇌. An irreversible reaction proceeds in the forward direction only and is shown by →.

rubric.why: The direction of reaction is the main test for reversibility.
rubric.description: Identifies that a reversible reaction proceeds in both directions.
rubric.how: Mention both forward and backward reaction.

rubric.why: The textbook definition specifies that both directions occur under the same conditions.
rubric.description: Includes the same-conditions feature.
rubric.how: State that the reaction proceeds both ways under the same conditions.

rubric.why: This distinguishes an irreversible reaction from a reversible one.
rubric.description: Identifies that an irreversible reaction proceeds forwards only.
rubric.how: State that it moves in the forward direction only.

rubric.why: The correct arrow symbols show the two types of reaction.
rubric.description: Gives the correct symbols for reversible and irreversible reactions.
rubric.how: Use ⇌ for reversible and → for irreversible.

modelAnswer: A reversible reaction proceeds forwards and backwards under the same conditions and is shown by ⇌.
An irreversible reaction proceeds in the forward direction only and is shown by →.

written.text: Do the phase changes in water (solid to liquid, liquid to vapour) reversible or irreversible?
written.finalAnswer: The phase changes in water are reversible. Ice can melt to liquid water, and liquid water can freeze back to ice; liquid water can evaporate to vapour, and water vapour can condense back to liquid.

rubric.why: The answer must correctly classify the phase changes.
rubric.description: States that the phase changes are reversible.
rubric.how: Clearly give the classification.

rubric.why: This gives one phase change and its reverse.
rubric.description: Explains melting and freezing as reverse changes.
rubric.how: Give the solid-to-liquid change and its reverse.

rubric.why: This identifies the liquid-to-vapour change.
rubric.description: Explains evaporation from liquid water to vapour.
rubric.how: Name the liquid-to-vapour direction.

rubric.why: The reverse phase change confirms that the change is reversible.
rubric.description: Explains that vapour can condense back to liquid water.
rubric.how: Name the reverse of evaporation.

modelAnswer: The phase changes in water are reversible.
Ice melts to liquid water, and liquid water freezes back to ice.
Liquid water evaporates to water vapour, and water vapour condenses back to liquid water.

written.text: How can a reversible reaction be forced to go to completion?
written.finalAnswer: A reversible reaction can be forced to go to completion if one of its products is withdrawn from the reaction mixture or, if the product is a gas, it escapes into the atmosphere.

rubric.why: Withdrawing a product is one of the two methods described in the section.
rubric.description: Explains that a product can be withdrawn from the reaction mixture.
rubric.how: State that removing one product drives the reaction to completion.

rubric.why: A gaseous product escaping also prevents the backward reaction from restoring it.
rubric.description: Explains that a gas product can escape into the atmosphere.
rubric.how: Mention escape of the gaseous product.

rubric.why: The answer must link the methods to the required outcome.
rubric.description: States that these changes force the reaction to completion.
rubric.how: Connect removal or escape of product with completion.

modelAnswer: A reversible reaction goes to completion if one of its products is withdrawn from the reaction mixture.
If a product is a gas, it can escape into the atmosphere as soon as it is formed.
The reverse reaction is then prevented, and the reaction is forced to go to completion.

written.text: Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?
written.finalAnswer: Copper sulphate pentahydrate is blue because it is hydrated. On heating, it loses water and forms white anhydrous copper sulphate. The change is reversible: anhydrous copper sulphate absorbs moisture and turns blue again.

rubric.why: The observation that hydrated copper sulphate is blue is central to the investigation.
rubric.description: Identifies the blue colour of hydrated copper sulphate.
rubric.how: State that the hydrated salt is blue.

rubric.why: The salt's hydrated form contains water of crystallisation.
rubric.description: Connects its hydrated form with water.
rubric.how: Mention that copper sulphate pentahydrate contains water.

rubric.why: Heating removes water and explains the change in colour.
rubric.description: Explains that heating drives off water.
rubric.how: State that the hydrated salt loses water on heating.

rubric.why: This names the product and its observed colour.
rubric.description: Identifies white anhydrous copper sulphate as the product.
rubric.how: Give both the product and its colour.

rubric.why: The reverse change demonstrates that the colour change is reversible.
rubric.description: States that anhydrous copper sulphate absorbs moisture and turns blue again.
rubric.how: Explain the return to the blue hydrated form.

modelAnswer: Copper sulphate pentahydrate is blue and contains water.
When it is heated, it loses water and forms white anhydrous copper sulphate.
CuSO₄ · 5 H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(g)
White anhydrous copper sulphate absorbs moisture from the atmosphere and turns blue again.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask you to define or distinguish reversible and irreversible reactions. State the direction or directions of reaction clearly.
For a symbol question, use ⇌ for a reversible reaction and → for an irreversible reaction.
For a longer explanation, earn marks by giving the observation, the change in substances, and the reason a product can or cannot react back.
For calcium carbonate in an open container, mention that carbon dioxide escapes; in a closed container it can react with calcium oxide to give back the reactants.
For hydrated salts, include both the colours and the effect of heating or moisture: hydrated copper sulphate is blue and anhydrous copper sulphate is white.

hints: Think about what the blue copper sulphate contains.
On heating it loses water; name the white product and say what happens when it absorbs moisture again.

steps.why: This equation is the textbook's example of a reaction that proceeds forwards only.
The textbook says the reaction goes to completion when stoichiometric amounts are used.
This conclusion follows because the reaction moves in the forward direction only.
steps.text: Such a reaction is called an irreversible reaction.

example.question: Use the reaction NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) to identify whether the reaction is reversible or irreversible.
example.answer: It is an irreversible reaction; it goes to completion and moves in the forward direction only.

explain.title: Irreversible reactions
explain.body: An irreversible reaction moves in the forward direction only. The textbook's example is the reaction between aqueous sodium chloride and silver nitrate, which goes to completion.

explain.title: Reversible reactions
explain.body: A reversible reaction proceeds forwards and backwards under the same conditions. Its products can react among themselves to give back the reactants. The symbol ⇌ has two half arrowheads pointing in opposite directions.

explain.title: Open and closed containers
explain.body: If a product is removed, or a gas escapes into the atmosphere, a reversible reaction may be forced to go to completion. In a closed container, the gas can remain and react back.

explain.title: Reversible changes in hydrated salts
explain.body: Heating blue hydrated copper sulphate forms white anhydrous copper sulphate and water. Anhydrous copper sulphate absorbs moisture and turns blue again. Heating pink cobalt chloride hexahydrate forms blue anhydrous cobalt chloride; with limited moisture it can form a purple dihydrate, and with more moisture it can form the pink hexahydrate.

mistakes: Do not use → for a reversible reaction; use ⇌.
Do not describe a reversible reaction as one that must go to completion. It can proceed in both directions under the same conditions.
Do not say that a product escaping promotes the backward reaction. An escaping gas cannot react back in the container.
Do not confuse the hydrated and anhydrous colours: hydrated copper sulphate is blue and anhydrous copper sulphate is white.
Do not confuse cobalt chloride colours: anhydrous is blue, the dihydrate is purple, and the hexahydrate is pink.
